newsitem.title: INDIA: India's BJP sets sights on early polls.
newsitem.headline: India's BJP sets sights on early polls.

text.p: India's rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday set the stage for a bid for power, saying it would vote out Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government with an eye towards early elections.
The main opposition party held talks with its key regional allies on Friday shortly before the lower house was scheduled to start debating a motion of confidence in Deve Gowda.
"There is no question of saving this government," BJP general secretary Venkaiah Naidu told Reuters.

The party, which won about a quarter of the votes in the last elections only a year ago, sought to allay fears in India's worried business community by promising to help pass an interim budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) after Friday's vote.
"We are a responsible party," said BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj. "We can't trifle with the economic agenda of the nation."
"But first things first," she told Reuters. "This government has to go."
The BJP ruled India for 12 days in May when President Shankar Dayal Sharma invited it to form a government as the largest party following inconclusive elections.

But its 193 deputies, including allies ranging from former Sikh separatists to socialist rebels of Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party, could not muster a majority in the 542-member Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament. That triggered its early fall.

Deve Gowda's United Front alliance stepped in to fill the breach, winning the Congress party's support on a platform of keeping out the BJP, accused by opponents of favouring India's Hindu majority at the expense of minority Moslems.
"The government will go today and that will be the end of their anti-BJP alliance," remarked K.L. Sharma, a party spokesman.
"We must pass the vote on account after that," he said, referring to the interim budget which would keep government programmes going until a new government was established.

Sharma said the BJP did not have enough support in parliament to stake a claim for a second term. BJP officials said the Hindu party was hoping for snap polls which surveys indicated would strengthen the BJP's hand in parliament.
"If something happens after the vote, we'll see about that," Sharma told Reuters.

Share prices on Indian bourses have risen and fallen in line with expectations about whether the investor-friendly budget proposed by Deve Gowda's government would survive the political crisis, which entered its 13th day on Friday.
The budget, which has yet to clear parliament, would slash corporate and personal income tax rates, and was expected to draw large amounts of fresh investment into stock markets and corporations.
The BJP has traditionally taken hardline stances in its election manifestos, vowing to build nuclear weapons and to protect domestic industry from foreign competition.
But during its brief stint in power last May, the BJP adopted a more cautious stance.
Atal Bihari Vajpayee, who served as prime minister during the BJP tenure, backed off from the hardline pro-nuclear stance.

His government advocated protecting India's consumer goods and insurance sectors from foreign competition, but otherwise broadly followed the liberal economic policies introduced by the preceding Congress-led government.
